question: The standard frequency of a large aircraft's constant-frequency AC supply is 400 Hz. The duration of one cycle is:

options.text: 4 milliseconds
0.4 milliseconds
2.5 milliseconds
25 milliseconds

explanation: Period = 1 / frequency = 1 / 400 = 0.0025 s = 2.5 ms.

question: The RMS (root mean square) value of an alternating current is:

options.text: The average of all the instantaneous values over a complete cycle
The difference between the positive and negative peak values
The DC value that would give the same heating effect
The maximum instantaneous value reached in each cycle

explanation: RMS is the 'effective' value that makes AC and DC directly comparable for power. Over a full cycle a sine wave averages zero, so the plain average is useless for power; the peak overstates it.

question: The aircraft AC phase voltage is 115 V RMS. The peak value of this sine wave is approximately:
explanation: Peak = RMS × √2 ≈ 115 × 1.414 ≈ 162.6 V. 81 V is the result of multiplying by 0.707 instead of dividing; 200 V is the line voltage of a star-connected system, a different thing.

question: A sine wave has a peak value of 100 V. Its RMS value is approximately:
explanation: RMS = 0.707 × peak = 70.7 V. 63.7 V is the average value of a half cycle (0.637 × peak).

question: Unless otherwise stated, AC voltages and currents quoted on aircraft equipment and in system descriptions are:

options.text: Average values
Peak values
Peak-to-peak values
RMS values

explanation: RMS is used because it relates directly to power and heating, so '115 V AC' means 115 V RMS — the value a typical AC voltmeter is calibrated to show.

question: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current:

options.text: Lags the voltage by 180°
Is in phase with the voltage
Leads the voltage by 90°
Lags the voltage by 90°

explanation: The inductor's back-EMF opposes changes in current, so the current reaches its peak a quarter of a cycle after the voltage. The memory aid 'ELI the ICE man': in an inductor (L), voltage (E) comes before current (I); in a capacitor (C), current comes before voltage.

question: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current:

options.text: Lags the voltage by 90°
Leads the voltage by 90°
Leads the voltage by 180°
Is in phase with the voltage

explanation: Charging current is greatest when the voltage is changing fastest (as it passes through zero) and zero when the voltage is at its peak, so the current peak occurs a quarter of a cycle earlier — it leads.

question: The frequency of the supply to a pure inductor is doubled. Its inductive reactance:

options.text: Increases fourfold
Halves
Doubles
Is unchanged

explanation: XL = 2πfL, so reactance is directly proportional to frequency. An inductor opposes rapid change, so it opposes higher frequencies more — and to DC (zero frequency) it offers only its wire resistance.

question: The frequency of the supply to a capacitor is doubled. Its capacitive reactance:

options.text: Falls to a quarter
Halves
Is unchanged
Doubles

explanation: XC = 1/(2πfC), so reactance is inversely proportional to frequency. A capacitor passes high frequencies easily and blocks DC (zero frequency) completely once charged.

question: A series AC circuit has a resistance of 30 Ω and an inductive reactance of 40 Ω. Its impedance is:
explanation: Resistance and reactance are 90° apart, so they add as the sides of a right-angled triangle: Z = √(30² + 40²) = √2,500 = 50 Ω. Simply adding them (70 Ω) ignores the phase difference.

question: A 100 V AC supply is connected to a series circuit with a resistance of 30 Ω and an inductive reactance of 40 Ω. The current is:

options.text: 2 A

explanation: Impedance Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, so I = V/Z = 100/50 = 2 A. 3.33 A and 2.5 A come from dividing by R or by X alone.

question: Power factor in an AC circuit is defined as:

options.text: RMS voltage multiplied by RMS current
Reactive power (VAR) divided by true power (W)
True power divided by apparent power (cos φ)
Peak voltage divided by RMS voltage

explanation: Only the in-phase part of the current does useful work. PF = W/VA = cos φ = R/Z. A purely resistive load has PF 1; a purely reactive one has PF 0.

question: A load draws 2 A from a 100 V AC supply with a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The true power consumed is:
explanation: Apparent power = V × I = 200 VA. True power = VA × PF = 200 × 0.8 = 160 W. The remaining reactive power is √(200² − 160²) = 120 VAR — it circulates between source and load without doing work.

question: AC generators are rated in kVA rather than in kW because:

options.text: kVA is the true power that the generator can convert into useful work
They can only supply purely resistive loads
Their heating depends on current, whatever the load's power factor
kW ratings apply only to DC machines

explanation: A low power-factor load draws more current for the same useful power. The generator's windings heat according to that current, so its limit is set in volt-amperes. A 90 kVA generator at PF 0.8 delivers at most 72 kW.

question: A purely inductive load connected to an AC supply consumes:

options.text: No true power: the energy it stores is returned to the supply
Its full apparent power, all of it converted to heat
True power exactly equal to its reactive power
Twice the power of an equal resistive load

explanation: With the current 90° behind the voltage, the power is positive for one quarter cycle and negative for the next, averaging to zero. Only the resistance in a real inductor consumes true power.

question: A series circuit of resistance, inductance and capacitance is at resonance when:

options.text: XL equals XC, so impedance is at a maximum and current a minimum
XL equals XC, so impedance is at a minimum, equal to R
R equals the sum of XL and XC, so the current is maximum
XL is twice XC, so impedance is at a minimum, equal to R

explanation: At resonance the two reactances cancel, leaving only R. Current is therefore at its maximum and in phase with the voltage. A parallel tuned circuit behaves the other way: maximum impedance at resonance — the basis of radio tuning.

question: Raising the supply frequency above the resonant frequency of a series LC circuit makes the circuit behave:

options.text: Inductively, with the current lagging the voltage
Capacitively, with the current leading the voltage
As an open circuit, with no current
Purely resistively, with the current in phase

explanation: Above resonance XL (rising with f) exceeds XC (falling with f), so the net reactance is inductive and the current lags. Below resonance the circuit is capacitive.

question: In a three-phase supply, the three phase voltages are:

options.text: Different in magnitude but all in phase
Equal in magnitude and displaced from each other by 90°
Displaced by 60°, with the third phase the sum of the other two
Equal in magnitude and displaced from each other by 120°

explanation: Three windings spaced 120° apart on the generator produce three sine waves 120° apart. Three-phase gives more power for a given weight of generator and cable, and naturally produces the rotating field induction motors need.

question: In a star (wye) connected three-phase system with a phase voltage of 115 V, the line voltage is:
explanation: Line voltage = √3 × phase voltage = 1.732 × 115 ≈ 200 V. That is why aircraft supplies are described as 115/200 V, 400 Hz, three-phase.

question: In a star-connected three-phase system:

options.text: The line current equals the phase current, and the line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage
Both line voltage and line current are √3 times the phase values
The line voltage equals the phase voltage, and the line current is √3 times the phase current
Line and phase values are equal for both voltage and current

explanation: Each line is in series with one phase winding, so the currents are the same, while each line-to-line voltage spans two windings 120° apart, giving √3 × phase voltage. In a delta connection it is the other way round.

question: A delta-connected three-phase system differs from a star system in that:

options.text: Line and phase voltages are equal and there is no neutral
The line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage, with a neutral
It can only supply single-phase loads from its windings
Its phase windings are displaced by 90° instead of 120°

explanation: In delta each winding is connected directly between two lines, so line and phase voltages are equal; each line current is the phasor sum of two winding currents, giving √3 × phase current. With no common star point there is no neutral.

question: Aircraft AC generators are normally star-connected with the star point earthed to the airframe. One advantage of this is that:

options.text: The line current is reduced to one third of the phase current
Both 115 V (phase) and 200 V (line) supplies are available
The generator produces direct current as well as alternating current
No circuit protection is needed on the single-phase loads

explanation: With the neutral earthed, single-phase loads connect between one phase and structure (115 V), while three-phase loads use the lines (200 V).

question: In a perfectly balanced star-connected three-phase load, the current in the neutral is:

options.text: Three times the current in one phase
Equal to the current in one phase
Zero
√3 times the current in one phase

explanation: Three equal currents 120° apart add to zero at every instant. The neutral only carries current when the phase loads are unequal, which they usually are to some extent in an aircraft.

question: A balanced three-phase load takes 100 A per line at a line voltage of 200 V and a power factor of 0.8. The true power is approximately:

options.text: 48 kW
16 kW

question: Large aircraft use AC as their main power supply mainly because AC:

options.text: At 115 V it cannot cause an electric shock to the crew
It is easily transformed and carried at higher voltage in lighter cables
It needs no circuit protection on its distribution wiring
It can be stored directly in the aircraft batteries for later use

explanation: Higher voltage means less current for the same power, and so thinner, lighter cables. Transformers convert AC to whatever voltage a load needs, and brushless AC generators avoid commutator wear. DC is still derived (via TRUs) for the battery and DC equipment.

question: Aircraft constant-frequency AC systems use 400 Hz rather than 50 or 60 Hz mainly because:

options.text: Transformers and machines can be much smaller and lighter
Batteries can be charged directly from a 400 Hz supply
Reactance and line losses are lower at higher frequencies
400 Hz is safer to touch than the lower mains frequencies

explanation: The iron needed in a transformer or machine falls as frequency rises, saving a great deal of weight. The penalty is that inductive reactance (and so voltage drop) is higher, which suits the short cable runs of an aircraft but would not suit a national grid.
